passage: Payal, come and sit. Vandana Aunty will tell you about her first Diwali. I was twenty-four. In front of ten guests my mother-in-law said my rotis were like leather. Everyone looked at me. My own sister whispered, "Say something back!" My face burned. But I said, "I'll learn from you, Ji," and passed the sabzi. I did not join the laughing, and I did not say a word against her. That night I told my husband Arun, "That hurt me in front of everyone. Help me think what to do." He spoke to his mother the next day, quietly. Things were not perfect after, but the guests never saw two women fighting, and Arun and I stayed on the same side. You don't have to swallow everything, beta. Choose where you say it.

qa.q: How many guests were at the Diwali meal?
What was Vandana feeling when everyone looked at her, and what cue does she give?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, since she says her face burned.

qa.q: What did Vandana do that night, and why might it help?
qa.a: She told her husband Arun privately that it hurt and asked for his help. A private talk keeps the couple on the same side without a public fight.

qa.q: Why might Vandana's sister have whispered "Say something back!"?
qa.a: Her sister probably wanted to defend her and saw silence as weakness, while Vandana chose not to answer sharply in front of guests.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how she avoided taking sides publicly against her in-laws and raised the hurt privately with her husband.

The power went out right as the Diwali dinner was served at Sachin's parents' house, and thirty relatives sat in candlelight around the long table.

In the dark, Sachin's aunt said loudly, "Devika, you still haven't learnt to make proper laddoos? In our family the daughters-in-law start early."

A few people laughed. Devika felt her face burn. She wanted to say that she ran a whole department at work, and that these laddoos were her first try.

Instead she said, "Next year you'll have to teach me, Bua," and passed the dish.

Sachin squeezed her hand under the table.

At midnight, driving home through the dark streets, she said, "That hurt, and it's not the first time. I didn't want a scene there. But I need you to speak to your Bua before Holi."

Sachin nodded. "You handled it better than I would have. I'll talk to her this week."

qa.q: What did Sachin's aunt criticise Devika for?
qa.a: The aunt criticised Devika for not having learnt to make proper laddoos.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when a few people laughed?
qa.a: Devika felt embarrassed and hurt, and wanted to defend herself.

qa.q: Why was Devika's choice of timing wise?
qa.a: She avoided taking sides against Sachin's family in public and raised the problem privately with Sachin on the drive home.

qa.q: How does Sachin see the situation by the end of the drive?
qa.a: Sachin respects how Devika handled it and accepts that he should speak to his aunt himself.

grounding: Shows a young wife avoiding public conflict with her husband's family and discussing the tension privately with her partner.

passage:
At Kamal's nephew's birthday party in their Kolkata building, his sister Rupa announced to the room, "Ira's still at that NGO? Must be nice, having a husband who earns properly."

Ira smiled politely and went to help cut the cake. Her hands were steady, but her chest felt tight. She could name five things wrong with Rupa's comment and one hurtful thing Rupa had said at their wedding.

She said none of them. She played musical chairs with the children, thanked Kamal's mother for the food and left with everyone else.

At home, Ira made two cups of tea and sat on the bed next to Kamal. "Can I tell you something that upset me tonight, just between us?"

He listened. Then he said, "She's been like that with me too. I'm sorry. What would help?"

"I don't need you to fight her. I just need you to know, and not laugh along next time."

"I won't," Kamal said.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling during the party, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ira felt hurt and tense; her chest felt tight though she smiled and kept her hands steady.

qa.q: What did Ira do that protected her marriage and the family peace?
qa.a: She didn't confront Rupa in public, and instead raised it with Kamal privately and asked for a specific kind of support.

qa.q: How does Kamal see his sister's behaviour?
qa.a: Kamal recognises it, saying Rupa has been like that with him too, and wants to support Ira.

grounding: Shows a young wife not taking sides against her husband's family in public and discussing the tension with him privately.
